clinicalPearls: Dilated portosystemic collateral veins in the rectum arising in portal hypertension
They are distinct from haemorrhoids, which are dilatations of the normal haemorrhoidal cushions
They appear as serpentine submucosal veins extending upward from the anorectum on endoscopy
They can cause significant, sometimes massive, lower gastrointestinal bleeding
Recognising portal hypertension is essential, as management differs from haemorrhoid treatment
Treatment targets portal pressure (for example with portosystemic shunting) alongside local haemostatic measures; conventional haemorrhoid procedures can provoke severe bleeding
reference.pathophysiology: Rectal varices form when portal hypertension drives blood through portosystemic collaterals between the superior rectal veins (portal system) and the middle and inferior rectal veins (systemic system). The resulting dilated submucosal veins can rupture and bleed. Unlike haemorrhoids, which are downward displacements of vascular cushions, rectal varices are true varices reflecting elevated portal pressure, so definitive control often requires reducing portal pressure rather than local excision.
additionalDifferentials: Other causes of lower gastrointestinal bleeding (angiodysplasia, neoplasm, diverticular)
additionalInvestigations: Endoscopic identification distinguishing varices from haemorrhoids
Assessment for portal hypertension and its cause (liver disease, portal vein thrombosis)
Cross-sectional or Doppler imaging of the portal system
Full blood count and coagulation/liver function tests
reference.prognosis: Bleeding can be controlled and prognosis is largely determined by the underlying portal hypertension and liver disease; recurrence is likely unless portal pressure is addressed.
pitfalls: Mistaking rectal varices for haemorrhoids and treating with banding or excision, risking severe bleeding
Failing to recognise underlying portal hypertension
Overlooking other bleeding sources in portal hypertension
references: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
management: Reduce portal pressure as the definitive strategy, with non-selective beta-blockers and treatment of the underlying liver disease
Achieve endoscopic haemostasis of bleeding varices with band ligation, sclerotherapy or coil-and-glue embolisation, avoiding conventional haemorrhoid procedures that can provoke severe haemorrhage
Resuscitate acute lower gastrointestinal bleeding with transfusion and correction of coagulopathy
Consider a transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt or interventional radiological embolisation for refractory or massive bleeding
Investigate and manage the cause of portal hypertension, such as cirrhosis or portal vein thrombosis
Multidisciplinary care with hepatology, interventional radiology and endoscopy, with surveillance for recurrent bleeding unless portal pressure is addressed
